embeds.title: Designing Analog Chips with AI Agents: Harald Pretl & Carsten Wulff
embeds.description:
Six months ago, AI models were scoring around 50% on Behzad Razavi's analog design benchmark. Now that benchmark is saturated. I talked to two experienced chip designers, Harald Pretl and Carsten Wulff, about what that actually means in practice.

Carsten is principal radio architect at Nordic Semiconductor and teaches advanced integrated circui...

messages.content:
I have to say, modern agent AIs are pretty awesome at smoke testing chips. My breakout board has a small MCU on it (acts as bootloader for my chip lol) and USB connection. So the test cycle is: write test for X functionality, transfer program to MCU, it flashes my chip then waits for response over serial, forwards back to PC for evaluation. The agent is slowly working through all the instructions and constructing tests for expected behavior and edge-cases. It also executes the tests against the RTL as a comparison.

Already found a few very silly bugs in the hardware (and confirmed a few I already knew about). I was going to do some of this testing for my self, but being able to automate testing of all major functionality is pretty rad

I wish I could do that risk-free with some HW I got where the PDF docs for the SPI interface's registers are wrong and I want it to run in Rust not C; sadly there's OTP on it and the host MCU on the boards can be bricked through fuses as well 🙁
oh boo, yeah that wouldn't be fun
luckily this thing is idiot proof and transient. if it gets wedged a power cycle forgives all sins 🙂
(otoh, it requires an MCU to be usable at all which was hilariously short sighted but oh well 😂 )
Yeah, I should still set it up get at least RADAR recording levels of capability implemented by christmas.

@BreakingTaps any hope of your works towards photodiodes becoming something we could put an experimental receiver on Run3? Like, some easy to demodulate scheme aimed at just pointing a multimode fiber at the die? I'm thinking like maybe Manchester or such.
i'm afraid I dont really have much done on that end 🙁 just a few quick "sketches" but never really got far enough to have anything approaching usable
i got distracted by other stuff and never got back to working on the photodiodes

From that works, did you catch info on the doping stuffs which would tell us if this linked paper might translate sufficiently-directly map to gf180mcuD? The structure they employ sounds quite useful. And they do get decent QE out of it (20%) even after accounting for the reflectivity loss and the metal obstructions.
I guess we might be more limited in how weak the "Isolated p - region" can be doped.
(Also I guess you were working on accumulation-mode self-integrating CMOS pixels rather than TIA-buffered high-speed receivers.)

Anyone have a setup to recommend where I could let Antigravity work on Rust/C/C++ code (which doesn't run on the host) to make an SPI transaction log of a Rust soft-MAC match the vendor SDK's SPI transaction log?

With a notable preference of mine towards needing fewer iterations, though tokens don't grow on trees:
it's just that I kinda have to review the code to check that it's not introducing behavior that (at a glance) causes writes to OTP or other irreversible actions like breaking my ability to access it through SWD (turn off reset pin, go to very deep sleep where SWD circuitry is too power gated to wake up from my programmer).
The other places I could easily ask seem to have turned to a hard anti-AI stance.

Huh, Antigravity comes with user namespaces based sandboxing...
Might suffice in place of some per-agent VM stuff and under sufficiently restrictive access to information.
